subject: Civil Engineering
title: Emerging Contaminants: PFAS and Microplastics
description: A short lesson to help you apply Emerging Contaminants: PFAS and Microplastics.

hook.text: PFAS chemicals are in the blood of 98% of Americans. They came through the water.

buildup.text: PFAS are 'forever chemicals' — they don't break down in the environment or human body.

discovery.text: Conventional treatment plants can't remove PFAS — granular activated carbon can.

twist.text: Microplastics pass through filters too. They carry toxins and enter the food chain.

climax.text: New EPA standards set PFAS limits near zero — treatment plants need expensive upgrades.

punchline.text: The contaminants we didn't know about are now the hardest to remove.

quiz.question: Why are PFAS called 'forever chemicals'?
options: They are found in every country on Earth
They do not break down naturally in the environment or human body
They have been used in manufacturing since ancient times

details.summary: Emerging contaminants including PFAS forever chemicals, microplastics, pharmaceuticals, and endocrine disruptors are found in water supplies worldwide at concentrations that conventional treatment cannot fully remove.
details.whyItMatters: PFAS and microplastics persist indefinitely in the environment and accumulate in living organisms. Regulatory standards are rapidly tightening as health effects become better understood, requiring water utilities to upgrade treatment systems.
takeaways: PFAS chemicals resist degradation and accumulate in human blood and organs over decades
Granular activated carbon adsorption is the most common PFAS removal technology
Microplastics are found in 83% of tap water samples worldwide according to research studies

faq.question: Why are PFAS called forever chemicals?
faq.answer: PFAS contain carbon-fluorine bonds that are among the strongest in organic chemistry, resisting biological degradation, heat, and chemical attack. Once released into the environment, they persist indefinitely, cycling through water, soil, and organisms without breaking down.

faq.question: Can conventional water treatment remove emerging contaminants?
faq.answer: Standard coagulation, sedimentation, and sand filtration remove less than 30% of most emerging contaminants. Chlorination can transform some pharmaceuticals but creates potentially harmful byproducts.
